en.title: Oscar Season Kicks Off: Venice Fest Signals the Start of the Race
en.summary: As summer blockbusters fade, a new race begins. The Venice Film Festival marks the official launch of Oscar season, bringing anticipation for the year's most acclaimed films.
en.body:
September traditionally signals a lull at the multiplex, with summer's biggest hits winding down and studios often releasing more niche genre films. But for those within the film industry, this quiet period is anything but. It marks the official commencement of Oscar season.

The year-round prognostication and blogging surrounding the Academy Awards never truly ceases, with the Sundance Film Festival kicking off the calendar in January, even as the previous year's awards race reaches its fever pitch. However, it's in September that the *real* momentum builds. This month hosts what can be considered the 'Big Four' film festivals, and it all begins with the venerable Venice Film Festival.

Founded nearly a century ago, the Venice Film Festival, while now a prestigious platform for cinematic excellence, has a complex history. Its co-founder, Giuseppe Volpi, was a fervent supporter of Benito Mussolini's regime, even naming the inaugural awards after the Italian dictator. Today, Venice stands as the first of a series of high-profile festivals, including the Telluride Film Festival, the Toronto International Film Festival, and others, all vying to showcase the films that will ultimately contend for Oscar glory.

## The Festival Gauntlet Begins

The Venice Film Festival, the oldest in the world, has once again set the tone for the upcoming awards cycle. Its programming consistently introduces films that capture critical attention and generate early buzz. Following Venice, the Telluride Film Festival, the Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF), and others continue this crucial unveiling process. These festivals are not just platforms for showcasing new cinema; they are the proving grounds where potential Oscar contenders are first seen by critics, industry professionals, and eventually, the public. Films like **Sinners**, **Frankenstein**, and **Marty Supreme** are among those generating early excitement, with **One Battle After Another** already earning accolades for Best Adapted Screenplay.

## What This Means for Fans

For passionate film fans around the globe, this festival season is an exciting prelude to the awards ceremony. It's a chance to discover the films that will dominate conversations for months to come and to form early opinions on potential nominees. The Academy Museum of Motion Pictures is already gearing up for the 98th Oscars®, offering immersive experiences and events that connect audiences with the history and magic of the awards. The anticipation builds towards the ceremony, which is scheduled for August 31, 2026, promising a showcase of the year's most impactful cinematic achievements.

## What's Next

As the festival circuit unfolds, keep an eye on emerging titles and early critical reactions. The slate for the 98th Academy Awards is starting to take shape, with more major festival premieres expected to reveal the films that will vie for the industry's highest honors.

content_raw: Early September is traditionally a quiet time at the multiplex. The last holdovers from the dog days of summer movie season—your Spider-Man s and Odyssey s, as well as August risks like Coyote vs. Acme —continue to do dwindling business. Meanwhile new and skewed genre films are taking their chances in the off-season. But for everyone else outside the industry, now’s the time to think about schools reopening and vacations ending. In the biz, though? This is among the most important weekends of the year! At last, Oscar season has come. As the cottage industry of year-round awards prognosticators and Oscar bloggers will attest, the rat race to the Academy’s big night never really stops, with the first major film festival of the year occurring at Sundance’s vaunted heights in the dregs of January, even as the previous year’s Oscar race rages on at its fiercest din. There is also the most prestigious fest of the year in the South of France: Cannes. But those events are by design (or posture) supposed to be above the fray of politicking and horse-racing. September, on the other hand, is the month where we get what could be called the Big Four, starting yesterday with the oldest film festival in the world: Venice. The Venice Film Festival was indeed a novel idea when it was co-founded nearly a century ago by Giuseppe Volpi—a devout fascist who was so enthusiastic about being minister of finance for Benito Mussolini that he named the first festival awards the “Mussolini Cup for Best Italian Film” and the “Mussolini Cup for Best Foreign Film.” Ah, history! These days Venice has a more respectable reputation as the first of virtually back-to-back events that also include the Telluride Film Festival (beginning on Sept. 4), the Toronto International Film Festival (Sept. 10), and the one I’ll eventually cover, the New York Film Festival (Sept. 25). Each has their own legacy and flavor that might be invisible to the casual observer, but they all amount to the building blocks necessary to create momentum in a campaign narrative (or collapse it in abject failure once the critics’ knives come out). Anora , the Best Picture winner from Sean Baker in 2025, premiered in May’s storied Cannes Film Festival but then built momentum at Telluride and Toronto in September. And while last year’s winner One Battle After Another loudly skipped the fests to have a wide U.S. release like a big damn Hollywood action movie, seven of the 10 Best Picture nominees still played in the September festivals, often more than one. Bugonia and Frankenstein even had their world premieres in Venice, Hamnet in Telluride, and Marty Supreme in New York. “I think for a filmmaker, you’ve got to just want to get into one, but there is prestige about certain ones that you want to debut and get your first eyes on you,” Clayton Davis, the chief awards editor at Variety , previously told me for Den of Geek magazine.
